name: Priya Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a normal workday look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the line crew that maintains the overhead circuits around our district. With my technical diploma and years on the truck, I usually take the awkward fault when two feeders meet, but I make everyone test the isolation independently. I like the quiet moment when the street lamps come back; I hate being told an office estimate is better than the crew’s measurements. My partner Mara and I have two children in school, a mortgage and about three months of expenses saved. I have never used an AI tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the forms can change if the office wants, but the crew still needs a paper record of the isolation point. The small time saving does not justify dropping a physical check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My pay is ordinary for a lead and our savings cover about three months, so the mortgage is not at risk from this little change. I do worry that someone will treat a typed summary as proof the wire is dead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the current testing sequence and ask for the printed switching sheet on every job. In the first year I would note any mismatch between the new form and the meter result, then raise it at our safety meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. I am bothered by careless paperwork, not by the idea of a quicker form.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What mismatch would you write down?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the form lists the wrong isolation switch, I would write its number beside the actual switch we tested. The crew would stop until the order was corrected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the software yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not for a small saving. I would read its output on the job sheet, but I have no reason to use an AI tool at home or on my own phone.

say: **Paper switching sheets** remain useful even if forms become faster.
**Physical checks** must settle whether a line is safe.
think: Our **three-month reserve** can absorb a minor office change.
A neat **typed summary** might be mistaken for proof of isolation.
do: **Keep** the current meter and isolation checks.
**Record** form mismatches and raise them at the crew safety meeting.
S0.quote: The small time saving does not justify dropping a physical check.
fieldNote: She has **never used AI** and sees no personal reason to start under a plateau.
Her **safety concern** is specific to switching errors, while household finances remain stable.

steps.text: Keep current meter and isolation checks on line jobs
Raise documented form mismatches at crew safety meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the office that dispatch software can draw a route, but a bucket truck still needs room and a crew still needs time to isolate. Our union should review any new repair targets before they take effect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The call desk could shrink while management asks my crew to cover more faults per shift. I have a few months saved and some other utilities nearby, but I do not want a lower overtime cheque creeping into the mortgage budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would log travel and isolation times for ten jobs, then give the log to our union representative. In the first year I would ask the representative to press for a crew-tested schedule and would keep my existing shifts while we wait for the result.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about what tighter schedules could do to our overtime. I can handle a changed timetable, but I do not trust a map that has never sat in the truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which route is the problem?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The lane behind the depot has a low bridge that keeps our bucket truck out. A car route looks fine on the screen and wastes half an hour for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the overtime cheque falls, what changes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mara and I would pause our planned kitchen work before cutting the children’s activities. I would not spend the three-month reserve to keep a renovation moving.

say: **Dispatch maps** need bucket-truck access checks before any proposed repair time becomes an official target.
**Union review** should precede new repair schedules.
think: A smaller **overtime cheque** could press on the mortgage budget.
Some **nearby utilities** exist, though a job change would still be disruptive.
do: **Log** travel and isolation times for ten line jobs.
**Give** the log to the union representative for a crew-tested schedule.
**Pause** kitchen work if overtime actually falls.
feel: **Anxious** about possible lost overtime and targets drawn without field knowledge.
S1.quote: A car route looks fine on the screen and wastes half an hour for us.
fieldNote: She defends **crew time** through a measured log rather than a general complaint.
Her **renovation pause** is conditional on lost overtime; current savings remain a buffer.

steps.text: Keep current shifts while logging ten repair times
Give ten-job log to union representative for schedule review
Pause kitchen work if overtime falls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would remind the crew that thinking AI arrives by 2028, while robots that can repair lines as well as us follow about 2031. There is a dangerous gap if the office starts writing jobs no person has checked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am a good lineworker, but a machine that can climb and repair would threaten my shifts after 2031. Our three months of savings would buy some time, not a second career, and only some nearby jobs are available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the union for a written agreement that field crews check AI work orders. If robots begin cutting repairs after 2031, I would apply for a nearby inspection job; until there is an actual offer, I would keep the mortgage buffer untouched and stay on the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed when I picture the robot taking the climb. I know what to do tomorrow at a pole; I do not know what my pay slip would look like three years later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a course immediately?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would ask which inspection jobs are open and whether training is paid before giving up a shift or paying a fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Mara at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show my partner Mara the dates and our three-month reserve. I would say we should pause the kitchen work if my hours are cut, not tell the children a job has already gone.

say: **2028 thinking AI** changes work orders before field robots arrive around 2031.
**Crew checks** are needed during the gap.
think: A capable **field robot** could reduce my repair shifts after 2031.
Our **three-month reserve** gives limited time to find another job.
do: **Seek** a union agreement for crew checks of AI work orders.
**Apply** for nearby inspection work if robots cut repair shifts after 2031.
**Pause** kitchen work if hours actually fall.
feel: **Alarmed** by possible loss of field income.
S2.quote: I know what to do tomorrow at a pole; I do not know what my pay slip would look like three years later.
fieldNote: She draws a clear line between **2028 office change** and later field robots.
She refuses a speculative **course fee** and would preserve savings until there is a real offer.

steps.text: Ask union for written crew checks of AI work orders
Apply for nearby inspection if robots cut shifts after 2031
Pause kitchen work if repair hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to demand a proper trial and a plan for crews before thinking AI reaches the office in 2031. The field robots come around 2034, and I want the safety representatives in the trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might accept a testing role, but I would need to see the equipment used on actual wires first. The children will be older and the mortgage may still be there; an abstract promise of a different job is not enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would join a union safety visit to a robot trial this year and write down each isolation check the machine fails. If the employer offers a local testing vacancy with paid hands-on training and a wage that covers our bills, I would take the training before 2031 and apply in the first year after 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but five years lets me see more than a brochure. I am willing to change for something that works in rain and wind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would convince you at the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A human crew should set a damaged-line task after bad weather and let the robot attempt it. I would want the stop button and failure log visible to everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the role pays less?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the offer with our fixed bills and refuse it if the gap ate our savings each month. My partner Mara and I would rather keep field shifts while they are available.

say: **Robot trials** need worker safety representatives before field deployment.
**2031 office AI** and 2034 field robots allow separate tests and decisions.
think: A **testing job** might work only after a credible field demonstration.
The **mortgage and children** require a wage that covers fixed bills.
do: **Join** a union safety visit and record failed isolation checks.
**Take** paid hands-on training only for a local bill-covering testing vacancy.
**Apply** for that testing role after 2031 if trained.
feel: **Anxious**, but open to change after a real field trial.
S3.quote: I am willing to change for something that works in rain and wind.
fieldNote: Her **resistance** softens when equipment is shown on a damaged line in rough conditions.
Her **training and application** depend on a local vacancy, paid practice and bill-covering wages.

steps.text: Join union safety visit and record robot isolation failures
Take paid testing training if linked to local bill-covering vacancy
Apply for testing role after 2031 if trained and wage covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade gives the company time to replace equipment carefully and let crews test machines before they touch the line. Thinking AI in 2036 and field robots around 2039 give us different dates to plan around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be fifty-three when the office changes, and I may still need years of wages after that. I will not assume our mortgage is paid or that a robot means I can retire; I would rather know the numbers each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay on the line crew and review the mortgage balance with Mara annually. In the first year after 2036 I would inspect any local safety testing vacancy and apply only if the duties are practical and the wage covers our bills; I would ask the union to keep a human stop rule in field trials.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Watchful but not frightened. A decade lets me weigh a safety testing job against the line crew I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the stop rule require?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Any crew member should be able to halt the robot and record why, without a manager clearing the log first. The trial should continue only after someone checks the hazard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move to get an inspection job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if Mara and the children could move without losing more than the new wage gains us. I would not uproot them for a vacancy I had not been offered.

say: **Field trials** need a crew stop rule before robots reach repair work.
**2036 thinking AI** and 2039 robots create separate planning points.
think: At **fifty-three**, I may still need wages and an unfinished mortgage.
A **local testing role** must be practical and pay enough before I switch.
do: **Review** the mortgage with Mara each year while keeping field shifts.
**Apply** for local safety testing after 2036 only if duties and pay work.
**Ask** the union to secure a human stop rule for robot trials.
feel: **Watchful**, with enough time to weigh real work options.
S4.quote: A decade lets me weigh a safety testing job against the line crew I know.
fieldNote: She rejects **automatic retirement** and any speculative household move.
Her **long-run plan** checks mortgage debt, wages, physical duties and a real vacancy before she accepts different work.

steps.text: Keep field shifts and review mortgage balance with Mara annually
Apply for local safety testing after 2036 only if duties practical and pay covers bills
Ask union for human stop rule in robot trials

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. We can cover a few months, but robots arriving around 2031 could still take a large share of our field shifts. A real local inspection opening with paid practical training and a crew stop rule would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who has the authority to refuse an unsafe work order. I expect the person at the line to keep the right to refuse an unsafe work order, even when it looks perfect on a screen.

portrait: **Priya Ibrahim**, 43, leads a power line crew and has a two-year technical diploma.
She has **two school-age children**, a mortgage, typical pay and roughly three months of expenses saved with partner Mara.
She has **never used AI**, prefers familiar checks and demands proof on actual equipment before changing her work.
She presses the **union** for repair time reviews, crew checks of work orders and a human stop rule.
The **2028 scenario** alarms her most; with more time, she considers testing work only under concrete pay and training terms.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** gives her little time before capable field robots could reduce repair shifts around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: A real **local testing job** with paid practical training and bill-covering wages would give her a credible route.
A written **crew stop rule** would protect workers during robot trials and field deployment.
headlineQuote: I expect the person at the line to keep the right to refuse an unsafe work order, even when it looks perfect on a screen.
